course.title: Russian Foundations
course.description: An original beginner sequence for A0 script and stress, followed by early A1 greetings and introductions, reviewed by a qualified Russian-language teacher. It is a practical first course, not a complete syllabus or an exam course.

units.title: Read the sounds
units.canDo: Read familiar Russian words, notice false friends, and read a few short phrases in the Cyrillic alphabet.

payload.title: Five familiar letters
lines: А, К, М, О, Т look like familiar Latin shapes.
Read these words slowly: ма́ма, кот, там, как.
Stress is marked with a small raised line over the stressed vowel: ма́ма. Words of one syllable, such as кот, там and как, carry no mark.

payload.title: Read the word
payload.instruction: Look at each word, then say it once aloud. The mark shows the stressed vowel.
lines: A vowel is not automatically stressed. Learn the marked word, not an imagined English sound.

payload.title: A word, not a list of letters
lines: Russian spelling is read letter by letter after a little practice.
The stress mark is a reading aid; it is not typed when you answer.
Say the word, then look again. Your first pass is allowed to be tentative.

responses.кот: Yes. кот means “cat”. The final т is hard: no soft sign or soft vowel follows it.

payload.title: В Н Р С У Х Е and lowercase п, и
lines: These shapes can suggest the wrong sound in English. В is not B, Н is not H, and Р is not P.
У looks like y but is /u/. Х is a /kh/ sound, not /h/.
Read the words as Russian spellings: рот, нос, сок, суп.

payload.title: Four look-alike words
payload.instruction: Read each word aloud. The English comparison is only a warning about the shape, not a translation shortcut.
lines: рот is not English “rot”; нос is “nose”; сок is “juice”; суп is “soup”.

payload.title: Trust the Cyrillic
lines: A familiar outline does not make a Russian word English.
Р is a rolling or trilled r; it is not the English p or r.
When a comparison helps, change the comparison as soon as you can and use the word in a real Russian phrase.

responses.нос: Correct: нос. Use it when you point to or discuss a nose.

payload.title: New shapes
lines: Б Г Д Ж З И Й Л П Ф Ц Ч Ш Щ Э Ю Я Ы add many sounds and endings.
Do not try to sound every letter perfectly today. Notice the shape, then meet the word.
И is like English i; Й is i with a breve and is a short glide. Compare и and й in the Reference.

payload.title: Words to recognize
payload.instruction: Read each word and notice its stress. These are small, useful words, not a complete vocabulary list.
lines: да and нет often answer a question. вот points to something nearby. банк and парк are everyday places.

payload.title: Words travel in phrases
lines: A word becomes useful when it meets a small phrase.
Я в ба́нке means “I am at the bank”; пойду́ в метро́ means “I will go into the metro.”
Learn the phrase shape now; leave the cases and verbs for their lessons.

responses.вот: вот means “here” or points to something nearby.

units.title: Greetings and introductions
units.canDo: Greet someone, say your name, introduce yourself politely, and ask someone to slow down.

payload.title: Greet before you ask
payload.instruction: Read each chunk as one gesture. Здра́вствуйте is a formal or general hello; приве́т is warm and informal.
lines: Choose the greeting that fits the person and setting. You do not need a translation before you greet.

payload.title: A greeting is a small conversation
lines: Здра́вствуйте is safe with an adult, a new acquaintance, or a group.
Приве́т is friendly and informal; it is not wrong, only a different register.
After a greeting, pause. The other person can answer before you continue.

responses.привет: Good choice: приве́т is the warm, informal hello.
responses.здравствуйте: That is a correct general or formal hello; it is more formal here.

payload.title: Choose the general hello
payload.prompt: Choose a safe hello for someone you have just met.

responses.здравствуйте: Yes. This is a neutral, respectful greeting.
responses.привет: This is friendly, but use it when the setting is informal.

payload.title: Name the person, then answer
payload.instruction: Read the chunks. Меня́ зову́т is the set phrase for giving a name (literally “they call me”); it is a complete, useful answer.
lines: Я студе́нт is a short statement: “I am a student.” Russian uses no word for “am” here; Я есть студе́нт is not said.

payload.title: No present-tense ‘to be’ here
lines: Russian does not normally use a present-tense verb equivalent of English “am/is” in these introductions.
Say Я студе́нт, not a literal Я есть студе́нт unless a teacher or text gives you that wording.
For a name, say Меня́ зову́т Анна. The name follows the phrase.

payload.title: Answer with your name
payload.prompt: How do you say “My name is …” as a chunk?

responses.как вас зовут: That asks someone’s name: Как вас зову́т?
responses.очень приятно: О́чень прия́тно means “very pleased” or “nice to meet you.”

payload.title: Ask politely
payload.prompt: Choose the question “What is your name?”

responses.как дела: Как дела́ is a broader “How are things?” greeting.

payload.title: Politeness in small chunks
payload.instruction: Read each phrase as something you could use with someone you meet or with a classmate.
lines: Повтори́те, пожа́луйста asks for a repetition. Говори́те ме́дленнее asks for a slower pace. Together they are a practical way to keep a conversation moving.

payload.title: Choose the tool for the problem
lines: Я не понима́ю says that you do not understand; it opens a request for help.
Повтори́те, пожа́луйста asks for a repeat; add Говори́те ме́дленнее, пожа́луйста when speed is the issue.
Извини́те is a polite “excuse me / sorry.” Use it before interrupting or making a small mistake.

payload.title: Ask for a repeat
payload.prompt: Choose the polite phrase for “Repeat, please.”

payload.title: Say when you do not understand

responses.очень приятно: That means “very pleased / nice to meet you.”

body.summary: In a simple introduction, Russian normally omits a present-tense ‘am/is’: Я студе́нт, ‘I am a student.’
lines: Меня́ зову́т… is the standard way to give a name.
The short statements and questions in Unit 2 are chunks to use, not a complete case system.

body.summary: The opening unit uses only a few high-value actions in set phrases.

lines: Здра́вствуйте / Приве́т
Меня́ зову́т…
Как вас зову́т?
Я не понима́ю. Повтори́те, пожа́луйста.

body.summary: Как вас зову́т? is a question about a person. The intonation work is introduced gradually; no audio is claimed here.
Numbers 1–10 are intentionally reserved for the next bounded unit. This pack is not a complete A1 syllabus.
The first words are kept in their lessons so the path, the Lexicon export, and the Reference share one identity.
